description_full: Kohl's Corporation operates as an omnichannel retailer in the United States. It offers apparel, footwear, accessories, beauty products, and home products through its stores and website. The company provides its products primarily under the brand names of Apt. 9, Croft & Barrow, FLX, Jumping Beans, SO, Sonoma Goods for Life, and Tek Gear, as well as LC Lauren Conrad, Nine West, and Simply Vera Vera Wang. Kohl's Corporation was founded in 1988 and is headquartered in Menomonee Falls, Wisconsin.
ceo_bio: Mr. Michael J. Bender | CEO & Director | Age 63 | Compensation: $5.3M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 84K people. Revenue per employee of $185K ranks in the bottom quartile among Consumer Cyclical peers. Each employee generates $12K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $405 per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 29× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (2/10).
financial_summary: Kohl's Corporation is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $2.6B market cap on $15.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -5% over the past three years and -2% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 10% against a 12% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 36%.

The business throws off $1.0B in free cash flow — roughly 6 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 5.07× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -8.3% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.6× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 2.1× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 2.1% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 4.2% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.5× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 4% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (8%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.49x its revenue share).
It accounts for 0.3% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 21% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 10% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 74% and a beta of 1.27, it amplifies market moves.
About $80.1M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 76% in the 2020 crash, 60% in the 2022 bear market and 54% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 68% below its DCF fair value of $71.01, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 54%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $57.46 to $89.93 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 9.9 vs 19.3, EV/EBITDA 7.0 vs 11.2 and P/FCF 2.6 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 20% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 38.6% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 12 covering analysts target $19.21 on average, 17% below the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 10% falls short of the cost of capital of 11.7%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.48).
It runs a 36% gross margin and converts 6% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: high accruals (-8.3% of assets).
ROE of 7% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (3.3x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.2% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.6x net debt to EBITDA ($674.0M of cash against $1.4B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.1x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.72 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -5.0% over 3 years, -0.5% over 5 years and -2.1% over 10 years, so the decline is deepening.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 10.1% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 0.1% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (2.4% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 6, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 85.8% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 4.2%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (5 sales, net $1.8M sold).
It returns 2.1% a year to shareholders (2.2% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 4.0% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 15 consecutive years, though it has been cut 12.3% a year over the last five.
Short interest is elevated at 34.1% of the float, 7.9 days to cover.
people: With about 84,000 employees, each generates about $185K of revenue, 0.5x the Consumer Cyclical median.
That works out to $12K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $5.3M (29x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
